utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alexis Demirdjian and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. Your Honours, with your leave, after the break, I'll be replaced by Mr. Hannis for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the witness escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bjelosevic. You may resume your seat and before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Bjelosevic, you told us that a member of the MUP had been prosecuted for crimes against non-Serbs. You couldn't remember his name but it was only a phone call away. Did you make the phone call overnight to find out what his name was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't understand I was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. I --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to return fairly briefly to the question of the relationship between the military and the MUP and in particular your relationship with General Lisica. It's right to say, wasn't it, that whatever the tone of the letters which were exchanged sometimes you and Colonel Lisica had a good relationship during 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did have some heated discussions about some matters, but our relationship certainly wasn't hostile. It was a relationship of co-operation. It was fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And would you agree with this: That you would occasionally visit police officers who were engaged under the military, and from time to time you would run into Colonel Lisica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you would have a conversation that went something like this: You would ask him how long he was going to keep your police officers there because you had better things to do?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we spoke about the situation on the battle-field, about problems in the rear, security-related problems. Those are mostly the matters that we discussed. I cannot recall the structure of our conversations and I cannot reproduce them, but these are the things that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And most of the time -- well, in fact, I would suggest perhaps all the time you found, between the two of you, a solution for any of the problems that might arise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we didn't identify problems, we acted pursuant orders. We could talk about various matters, but it was clear who the executive power of issuing orders had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, I want to -- to deal with this. You said effectively the military commander had the power to order anybody within his zone of responsibility. That's what you are saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in his zone of responsibility, the commander could issue orders and involve all structures in defence-related the matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that only, that principle only applied if there was the existence and declared state of war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, it was different, wasn't it, an imminent threat of war. There, isn't this right, Mr. Bjelosevic, the commander had the right to request from the ministry the use of police and other such people to help the military, but not actually to simply order, however Colonel Lisica may have phrased the requests?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Law on National Defence, in case of war and imminent threat of war, that is both, you can check that because you say you have a legal library, and the commander exercises power in accordance with that. He engaged those forces that under his estimate were necessary to defend the front line, and so on. You mentioned that the procedure should have been to apply for approval to the ministry, but that procedure was not prescribed by the law and it would have taken very long anyway. That area was always near the front line. It was very dynamic, and such a procedure would not have been appropriate if it had been necessary to wait. The commander exercised the power that he had under the law, and that's how things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelosevic, I hear what you say, but that is not, in fact, right, is it? It may have been that Colonel Lisica phrased his demands, as it were, as an order, but the reality is, wasn't it, that he had to ask you, and you didn't refuse, and if you had said no, then the issue would have had to have been resolved at the higher level by the Main Staff of the VRS and by the minister; isn't that the actual situation at this stage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the way I described it, and to clarify additionally, I can remind you of the situation in July when he ordered the entire police force from Derventa to be deployed at the front line urgently, in the direction of Brod. And I only learned about that later. In order to make sure that the situation in town and the surroundings be bearable, he ordered police forces from Prnjavor to take over policing tasks in town, and he said that he did so because things were urgent. He didn't even have time to call me or contact me, but issued a direct order. But to provide security to the town, he ordered police forces from Prnjavor to come and do policing work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to come on to that but I'll deal with it now. In Derventa, a town command was set up, wasn't it, because after the Serbs retook it, it was in, putting it colloquially, a terrible mess; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the colonel ordered that military administration be established and one of his assistants was appointed as town commander. I believe that we were able to see his order, the original order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. And the town command was also set up, actually, by him in Brod, wasn't it, Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Derventa -- or, rather, Derventa was in July and Brod was in October, but it wasn't a town command. It was a military administration headed by a military commander where he had his assistants as laid down by the commandant's order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But when a town command was set up because law and order and everything, all facilities, had broken down, the civilian police conducted their own affairs, didn't they, in the same way as they would in normal circumstances. In other words, they investigated robberies, murders, looting and the like; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. Military administration -- the phrase speaks for itself. It didn't provide for a full liberty to the civilian authorities, but we are speaking about a restrictive approach by all bodies involved and the imposition of such rules wherever there's most military administration. But during that period, at least, and that is until October, when we speak about the northern part, the forces spent most of the time at the front line. Some forces dealt with security and many staff were positioned at check-points. Much attention was devoted to the prevention of looting. Looted goods should be seized, taken away. Those were their instructions, anyway, and they were supposed to issue certificates for seized goods, and then arrangements would be made as to what should happen to those goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've mentioned check-points. I haven't finished what I want to ask you about commands, but is it right that General Lisica complained to you, or brought to your attention, that these check-points being manned by the police were actually not stopping people with loot, but were effectively taking bribes and letting them through? Is that right or wrong? You can answer that fairly simply.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've reminded me of something that really happened on several occasions, and please allow me to explain. At the briefings to which I was often invited at the command, we discussed the issue of looting, and Commander Lisica often asked me, What's your force doing, why don't they prevent looting? And I tried to explain what was really happening in practice, that people in uniform are looting and that they are armed and that it was a problem, that there had been conflicts and weapons pointed at people, and so on. On one occasion, I was on my way to the barracks at Derventa where a briefing was called, and I was passing through town and saw at various places that people in military uniforms were loading some goods from houses on to trucks, and so on. When I came to the barracks, I saw Colonel Lisica and told him what was happening, and I suggested to him that we should take a ride through town for him to see what is happening. And then at some places he got out of our vehicle and ordered those persons to produce their ID. They -- and when we got back to the barracks, he was extremely furious. He shouted at the military police and gave them orders to act, and so on. So what you are saying is correct, but what I said is also true and he started to view things a bit differently once he had seen the situation with his own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Can I just complete, please, what I want to put to you about town commands. That a town command was a temporary body that existed until civilian life returned to normal; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was up to the commander to lift military authority and re-establish civilian authorities. That was based on his estimate of the situation, but it was entirely up to him to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And finally this: The town commander would co-ordinate the tasks to be done by the police and other bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, in the order about the setting up of military administration, the town commander was the person who gives orders and co-ordinates activities. I believe you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally on the question of the military and police relationship, disciplinary matters. When you were asked about this by Mr. Zecevic, you stated that: From the moment when the police is deployed in combat - sorry, this is at page 19654 - it represents an element of the armed forces and subject to all rules and possibly disciplinary measures applied by the military because they are engaged in combat by the military. And you were saying that when you had a look at a document which is in the Defence bundle. It's 1D46 and it's at tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could have that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can the usher please help us with the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can see this is the order of the 15th of May of 1992 by Mico Stanisic. Go to the second page, and your direction was drawn -- your direction. Your attention was drawn to paragraph 8 where the order read: "In carrying out regular duties and tasks, the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs and other regulations of the Serbian Republic of BH currently in force shall be strictly upheld, whereas in military operations, military regulations and rules shall be enforced." And you said yes, that was your understanding, that if they were re-subordinated to the military, police would be disciplined by the military. But your attention wasn't drawn to the second part: "Any violation of regulations and failure to carry out tasks which have been ordered shall be subject to severe punishment and result in appropriate disciplinary and criminal sanctions." Now, you see, Mr. Bjelosevic, if what you are saying is correct and that the -- during re-subordination, the military dealt with discipline of the police, there would be no point, would there, in Mico Stanisic issuing this order, would there, before I put the next part to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are wrong. I'll try to explain. In the first subparagraph, I don't think that there's anything unclear. I believe that the language of this order is very clear here. The regular duties and tasks are one thing, whereas the police engaged in military operations is another thing. Military relations and rules are mentioned there. Whereas the other subparagraph about violation of regulations and failure to carry out tasks shall be subject to severe punishment and result in appropriate sanctions. I don't see what the problem is here. The minister orders what kind of conduct is appropriate in carrying out bigger tasks and duties, and also states what the situation is when the military --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: When the police is re-subordinated to the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he mentions sanctions and punishment. I don't see what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the issue is this: Because I suggest to you that contrary to your assertion, it was, in fact, the police chain of authority that at all times remained responsibility for disciplinary proceedings; whether or not at the time that the disciplinary offence was committed, or the criminal offence, the particular officer was re-subordinated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is clear which provisions of which law apply to a police officer at any given time, when the police officer carries out his regular tasks and duties or when he carries out military duties, when he is under military command. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you point me, please, Mr. Bjelosevic, to any provision of the law that says in terms during the period when an officer is re-subordinated to the military, it is the military who are responsible for conducting disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of joining a military formation, the police officer is subject to the military command and the military rules and regulations by the very fact that he has joined the military. Can I try to explain --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- by an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, all right, if it's an example that's right on point and short. Is this an example from something that actually happened or you are just speculating?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not speculation. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, before you go into a long example, is this an example of that you are going to give of something that actually happened. In other words, that a police officer whilst re-subordinated to a military command was disciplined by the military? If not, then I am afraid -- and you can be asked about it by Mr. Zecevic, then I don't want to hear about it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can immediately remember two examples. One is from September, I think, during the carrying out of combat operations in the direction of Brod. There was a slight confusion and unplanned retreat. Commander Lisica placed the commander of that police platoon in custody and remand prison. I don't know if I should mention his name because he is a high-ranking police official nowadays. And he was in remand prison for 24 hours. And the other case is from 1994. The incident happened on Mount Ozren near Vozuca. The front line was being pierced and some people went AWOL, and a number of police officers were sanctioned. Although I was in Bijeljina already, it was in autumn, I know that the military police arrested them, and they were detained for awhile. When I arrived at the command post, we calmed down the situation and the people were returned to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I am sorry, who conducted it? It may well be that Colonel Lisica in a fit of rage put somebody into prison for 24 hours. Who conducted any proceedings against him? And you better tell us the name of this man, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Having regard to the witness's comment about the present status of that man, shouldn't we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours, if you think that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On two occasions, police officers were incarcerated for a period. Who actually conducted any disciplinary or criminal proceedings against any of these people, or were there none?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first case, the measure was imposed by Commander Lisica. The second time on Mount Ozren, it wasn't him. But let me explain this one thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I want know, you've said they were arrested. That's not the same thing. I want to know if any proceedings, either disciplinary or criminal, were carried out against any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military has a different way of functioning, and that's what I'm trying to explain. It's the commander who is in charge in peacetime when you would do your national service. An officer would have the right to send you, for up to seven days, to military detention without any proceedings being conducted. The military functions in a different way compared to the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I suggest to you that these examples are really not appropriate to the principle which I'm putting to you, and I've already put it to you and you disagree, which is that the -- even when the police are re-subordinated, it is the police who are responsible for taking proceedings. Now, can I ask you, do you know somebody called Ljubisa Kitanovic? Let me make sure I've got the right name.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Kitanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just let me double-check the name. Ljubisa, yes, Kitanovic, also known as Crni?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crni, didn't he have some other name in Samac? I can't remember it now. But I believe that in Bosanski Samac, there was a man nicknamed Crni, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only heard that he was in Samac. I think that Crni is mentioned also at the time of the blockade of the corridor. That name was mentioned quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is a different Crni. This is -- do you know anything about a man called Ljubisa Kitanovic? Do you have any dealings with a man called Kitanovic, born in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember anybody by that name right now. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you ever made aware of any allegations made against you by this man?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with two matters, finally, quite shortly. I want to ask you for your view, as chief of the CSB for quite a long period, about this: If you received credible information that police officers from an SJB that came within your area of responsibility had killed over 100 unarmed men, would you feel it was your responsibility to make sure that those responsible for the killing were immediately arrested and questioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's an issue of interpretation. I'm a bit confused now. If I understood you correctly, you are speaking hypothetically, had there been 100 murders by a policeman, would such a policeman be arrested?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, that's right. I'm asking you, if you received credible information that police officers from an SJB that fell within your area of responsibility had murdered in one incident over 100 people, would you feel it was your responsibility to make sure that these men were immediately arrested and questioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, had I had such information, I would probably do exactly that. Of course it all depends on circumstances, where they are, who they are, what kind of danger there is, but of course there would be some efforts in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you think it appropriate for the chief of the SJB to immediately send those police officers as a unit to the army so that it became difficult to question them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If police officers under your direct command, Mr. Bjelosevic, in other words, someone you had direct control of, not through an SJB chief, went to a prison and forced the prison authorities to release some other policemen, one of their number, would you think it was appropriate to investigate that matter and question those police officers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are talking about an assumption. Some policemen were detained, and then some other policemen came to take them out of detention using force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely also a breach.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which should have been investigated. If it had happened to you by -- you should have ordered the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander should have reacted, chief of the station, and anybody else who had such information. I absolutely agree that the reaction should have been made immediately, if such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, if barricades had been erected throughout the town of Doboj before any conflict broke out, and armed men were stopping people at these barricades and surrounding municipal buildings, would you think it appropriate that you should use the police to remove these people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, it's all hypothetical. You say if this happens, if that happens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking for your understanding and reaction as a chief of a CSB. Would you have thought that it was proper to allow armed men to set up barricades in the town of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a connection with reality, with practice here. Barricades were erected at various points in March already, as well as national roads and approaches to certain settlements. If we talk specifically about Doboj, in April there were already some barricades and I think I spoke about that. Such barricades would be put at around sunset at the approaches to Carsija and Gradina and other places, and not even regular police patrols would be able to pass. It was quite clear who was able to enter that area, who would be accepted by people manning those barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking -- may I make this clear, I'm not talking about barricades at various ethnically separate parts of the town. I'm talking about barricades being erected in order to make demands to the municipal leadership. Totally different situation.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's hypothetical assumption. We should consider a number of elements: What it is about, in which municipality, why the barricades were erected, who erected them, were they armed or not? This is all about careful estimate and evaluation of the situation, and only then can you choose an appropriate measure of reaction. What were the circumstances, was it peacetime, war time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, one last question and then we'll leave this topic. If the barricades, to your certain knowledge as a police officer and from the information you got, were being put up by criminals, well known criminals, would that make a difference?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are still talking about the same hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to know whether that would make any difference to what you would do. If the answer is no, then say so.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I should consider a number of various elements in order to evaluate the situation. Right now, I know nothing. This is just a hypothetical: Barricades set up, municipality blockaded, we don't know who it is, what were the reasons, are they armed are not, are there any people armed within the municipality building, are we dealing with a hostage situation, what are the elements? It all really requires a careful evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I won't pursue this. Final question on factual matters before I deal with the very last topic. In 1994, or thereabouts, were you ordered by Mico Stanisic to solve the issue of the killings at Koricanska Stijena in 1992? And I use the word "solve."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992, Koricanska Stijena, that's something that happened outside the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB. But when Mr. Stanisic was minister again in 1994, I received another assignment from him. I had to go to Prijedor, I think it was sometime in April, and we had to resolve a situation of multiple murder. Sixteen or 17 people were killed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, this is a killing that took place in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. It's outside what we are concerned with. I simply want to know, whether at any stage, he ordered you to carry out further investigations and solve the killings which had occurred in 1992 on Koricanska Stijena?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, I want, just quickly, to ask you a few more questions about your time that you told us about with the military, in the period between the beginning of May and the end of June. And do you agree that your military booklet that you provided us with, and which we can see, it's 20096, tab 100. Do you have the original with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I brought it here, but it seems to have been left in my other jacket. Yes, I think I left it in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We are going to look at it on the screen anyhow.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought it here on Tuesday and Wednesday, and then nobody wanted to take a look at it, so I left it in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that we have on the screens the booklet. It's a personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it is. Quite right. 20129. Sorry. And it's tab 108. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that's a photocopy of your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the military booklet should record, is that right, the times when you do service with the military? For example, if we go to --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You agree. All right. It shows that you did your military service ... somewhere --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning with the 2nd of October, 1970, until the 13th of February, 1971, in Mostar, I was an intern because my national service was recognised as part of my university studies. And then I simply had to do an internship in order to be qualified for the position of an officer and the appropriate rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that -- it does show -- and I'd -- rather than go through all the pages, that you were shown to be fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's at page 3 in English and it's section 5 in B/C/S. That will be on the second page, I think. Third page. Is that section 5? No. It's going backwards, I think. Yes, sorry, it's page 2 in B/C/S. Yes, I think we are being shown it. Sorry, I didn't notice that. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows you were fit for military service on the 20th of September, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, then to section 6 which is at page 5 in English, and presumably the next page in B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Shows you were doing your military service between October 1974 to the 13th of February, 1985, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to page 8 and section 8 in B/C/S -- page 8 in English. And it's the fifth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see your various promotions, and I'm not going to trouble with them until we get to the -- next page in English, please, and the next ... by 1991, section 6, you've reached the rank of commander or captain, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now, finally, page 15 in English and section 10 in B/C/S; 10 in B/C/S. No, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows that your, as it were -- your military service was cancelled because you've gone to the MUP, is that right, between the 4th -- this is the -- obviously the RS MUP, between the 4th of April, 1992, to the 30th of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, wrong page in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is absolutely no record whatsoever in your military booklet of you being assigned to the military between April and end of June -- sorry, between May and the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My war time assignment was not changed. I was -- I remained with my previous war time assignment, but, during that period, I was re-subordinated, and that's something that is normally not recorded in the military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you say you were re-subordinated, and it wasn't recorded in your work booklet either, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not normally recorded in the work booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By whom were you re-subordinated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the command, the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps. Maybe I should explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. You've told us where you were. I understand where you say you were. I want to know, please, who ordered you to go and work under military command? Who? Not where, who?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one thing when there is a written order for somebody to be appointed to a position of command. That is done by a written order and that happened twice. I said once in spring. I think it was the end of May or the beginning of June, at the beginning of the operation called Corridor; and then the second time, it was in November 1992 when I was engaged to perform functions of the battalion commander. And in this interregnum, so to speak, there was no written order. I was engaged according to need. If at one point there was no CSB, then until my final appointment, I was engaged on various tasks that I already mentioned. And there wasn't a written order that applied to the whole of this period. That's what I'm trying to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, that's -- leave aside November. We perfectly accept what happened to you in November. I'm only interested in the major period, which, as you know, I put it to you before, is the period when all these crimes were committed in Doboj. Where is the order that you say re-subordinated you to the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this written order is. Whether I returned it with all other document when I was sending back the combat reports, that's probably how it happened, that is how it went back. If you are asking me who wrote that order, it was the corps commander, if I remember correctly, or maybe the Chief of Staff, but I think that it was commander who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The late General Talic, that's what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think that he signed the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you let Mico Stanisic know that in this early period of huge change, one of his chiefs of the CSB was simply not going to be there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Minister Stanisic about this engagement of mine when I attended the meeting. I had no opportunity to inform him about that prior to that. Even though the other day you put it to me -- you claimed that it was possible to go to Sarajevo -- to come from Sarajevo, that the communications were operational. But I would like that person claiming that it was possible to reach Sarajevo and Pale to show me which route was open. My position is that it wasn't possible to travel between Doboj and Pale. There were simply no roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may not have been possible, and leaving that aside for you to travel, you could, however, have sent a dispatch, couldn't you, to Mico Stanisic, via Banja Luka, as we saw you did before, saying, General Talic has asked me to come and work with the army because of operation corridor? You could have done that, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you even imagine what the situation was like there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just answer the question, please. Could you have sent a dispatch, as you sent a letter over this Dutch journalist, or dispatch, via Banja Luka to Stanisic saying, General Talic has asked or ordered that I go and work with him, is that all right? You could have done that, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even think about it at the time. In May, I didn't even know whether there were any links between Banja Luka and Pale at the time, and I don't think that those links existed continuously. I think that some links were established later on, that the army did it, and it worked only sporadically, as far as I know. But to tell you the truth, at that time, in the beginning, in the first half of May, it did not even occur to me that I would have to find, at any cost, a mechanism of informing the minister. Given the factual situation, given how things were, it was pointless for me to sit by myself, as a chief of CSB, alone in the office without having a single department operational. Facing the reality as it was, we were encircled. There were no goods in the shops, there was no money, no living conditions, basically, no electricity, no traffic, disorder in health services. If you can just imagine that situation, and people getting killed all around us and shooting everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have already been through the fact, Mr. Bjelosevic, some time ago that the MUP, both in the old BiH and the RS, was a strictly hierarchical disciplined body. Now, how could you possibly have disappeared off, as you say you did, without informing your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state was also organised in accordance with the constitution. It functioned in accordance with the constitution, and then it collapsed. The entire system collapsed. The communications collapsed, everything did. It will not be an exaggeration for me to say that there was this instinct for survival that prevailed for personally and for the family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Bjelosevic. Instinct for survival for you and the family. You just effectively abrogated your responsibilities, didn't you, to Mr. Petrovic and the SJB, and you effectively hid out to save yourself? That's what happened, isn't it, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. I would absolutely not agree that that is how it was and there's numerous evidence and numerous witnesses who can prove that that is not how it was, that I did not run off in that period of time. Had I run off, I would not have been awarded with the Karadjordje Star and I would not have received the veterans status. And it was not me who abrogated the responsibilities and who shifted the responsibilities to Mr. Petrovic. I explained to you what the circumstances were that led to this. And later on you could see how people interfered by way of orders, and later on the Crisis Staff verified this or ratified this officially. And I think that it was rational because only part of the territory of pre-war municipality of Doboj was under the control of the forces and that security station that existed was quite sufficient to deal with the security matters in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll make it quite clear. I'm sure you did go off to the military forward command from time to time, and that was your excuse, wasn't it, for not dealing with any of the matters, the crimes that were committed during that period? Do you understand, Mr. Bjelosevic? I suggest you hold full responsibility for what happened and that you were there more often than you are prepared to admit?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand your position, what you are claiming, but I disagree with you because that's not how it was. Second, I especially disagree with the last claim you uttered because that's not how it was under the law. The law regulates clearly what the responsibilities of the public security station and its territory, and for some reason you are putting it wrongly. I don't know why you are doing this because that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Bjelosevic, one follow-up question about this: You said you talked to the minister about your appointment in the army and your leaving your post as CSB chief. At the meeting, you said, could you remind us the date of that meeting you are referring to? What meeting are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting which took place on the 11th of July in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zecevic takes the floor, I, too, have a small question for you, Mr. Bjelosevic, namely in respect of the establishment of the town commands which you told us about earlier this morning. And my question to you is: Where these town commands were established, were there also in these towns or municipalities Crisis Staffs existing or established at the same time in any of the places where town commands were established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. During that period of time when the town command existed, it was, if I can put it that way, the sole authority. There were no Crisis Staffs or any other organs in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the town command or the town commands, did they include any representation from civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would have the town commander, and the town commander had his assistants for various matters. And it wasn't arranged identically in every town. Military administration existed in Brod, in Derventa, in Odzak. Odzak had the strictest term of military administration because there weren't many civilian residents there anyway and there were very few assistants for various matters. Whereas in Derventa and in Brod, there were more assistants of the town commander for various matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Just to be clear about what your testimony is: When you say that the town commander had assistants, would these assistants be recruited from his own military staff or would they be recruited from civilian authorities? In other words, what I'm interested to know, Mr. Bjelosevic, is whether the town commands were exclusively military bodies, or whether they were bodies that were chaired by a military commander but also included civilian representatives from the local area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I fully understood your question. In Odzak, it was an exclusively military administration comprising military officers. In Derventa, some assistants appointed by the operative group command were assistants to the town commander. And if I can remember, one of them was a woman, and then there were also military officers among them. So it was mixed, there were some civilians in charge of certain matters. I think that this lady was in charge of legal affairs or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyway, they are outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. Do you remember, there is a document on the Derventa town command. It was actually shown to one of the witnesses or maybe more than one which sets out who it is. For the moment, I can't remember the number but if I do, I'll remind Your Honours are that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I do remember the document, I just wanted to have this witness's explanation. Thank you very much, sir. Back to you Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I propose that we adjourn at this point and that I start re-examination -- redirect examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, Mr. Zecevic, how long do you anticipate that your re-examination would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very hard for me to say, Your Honours, because I anticipated at the beginning of today -- I anticipated around two, two and a half hours, but now there has been some other matters. So I'm really not sure. I have to review during the break the transcript and see what else do I need to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The practical question I'm really thinking about is in terms of your next witness, whether we should be thinking in terms of him tomorrow morning or later this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honours, I anticipated this situation, and I already scheduled the witness for tomorrow morning, yes, the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, I just want to indicate I am Tom Hannis, now appearing in place for Ms. Korner. And also, she asked me to request that 65 ter 20138, which is the document concerning criminal charges against Jozo Mandic, be tendered and marked MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how about the military booklet, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if that was not tendered, we would like to tender it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 20129 will become Exhibit P2344. And 65 ter number 20138 will become Exhibit P2345. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am sorry. Mr. Hannis offered the document P2345 as MFI, and I didn't object because that is the -- that is the practice that we adopted because all these documents are MFI'd pending the submissions. And the second document, 2344, which is a military booklet, I do not object, and that can be tendered in evidence. Can, please, the record reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so the -- you got that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P2345 is thus marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, good morning, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will first discuss with you the matters that you commented on during the first session with Ms. Korner, and then after that we will go back to the very beginning of your cross-examination and cover the matters that, in our opinion, Ms. Korner failed to touch upon. Sir, on page 3 of today's transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry. Based on that, I would like to impose an interjection at this point. If he is going to ask about matters that Ms. Korner didn't touch on, then I would say that is beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think Mr. Zecevic intended to say what he came across as having said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, precisely right. If you will remember, Ms. Korner on a couple of occasions stopped the witness during his answers as saying, You will deal with that with Mr. Zecevic. And that is what I intend to question the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 3, you replied to Ms. Korner's question by saying, Yes, in the area of responsibility, the commander can issue orders and order all structures on matters concerning defence. And then Ms. Korner, in line 16, suggested to you that that principle can be applied only when the state of war has been declared, and you disagreed with that. You said that the state of the imminent threat of war was identical in that sense. And I have one question concerning that. Mr. Bjelosevic, given the situation that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in May, April, and June of 1992, even though I think it prevailed throughout 1992, was that, according to you, a de facto state of war or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a state of war. It had all the features of the war conflict. It was just a matter of formal declaration of the state of war or imminent state of war. But formally speaking, given all its features, it was a proper war conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, Ms. Korner asked you about your relationship with Colonel Lisica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at tab 135 of the Defence binder. This is 1D263, tab 135. Defence tab 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, is this your letter sent to the command of the operative group of the Serb army under the command of Colonel Lisica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this letter, do you request that the police be withdrawn from combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for the commander's approval for the police to be withdrawn from combat action because of the deteriorating security situation. We needed these people in order to solve and stabilise the situation and the security concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 1D264 which is tab 231. Tab 231.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document, 231, or has something been mixed up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, tell me, please, what is this? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the reply of Commander Lisica to the letter which we just saw, to my letter, where he explains, saying, I understand your proposal concerning the withdrawal of police from combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in his position regarding your request that police be withdrawn. This is the penultimate sentence, or two sentences before the end.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see it in the middle. I do not authorise the withdrawal of police forces. He has the executive power in this situation and in many others. He made the executive decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that same sentence, he makes some comments about the territory. Can you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he says that he does not allow for the withdrawal to take place because otherwise the front would be moved close to Doboj very soon, and you will not have the territory to control at all. And then he goes on to say, I hope that you understood properly my reasons. And his reasons are fully justified. I completely understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm sorry but you mention tab 231 for this document, which is obviously -- well, the transcript mentions 231 which is obviously not the document we discussed about because it is said to be the international travel approval for Kreso [phoen], Ismet, 231. It's another -- I don't even have a 65 ter number for that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's already exhibited, Your Honours. It 1D264. I am sorry my tab numbers are mixed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1D264. That is the document that we have on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm informed is that this document was not on the Defence list of documents they were going to use with the witness. It was a document on the Prosecution's list, our tab number 119. 119. So I think that's why you can't find a Defence tab for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Mr. Hannis's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 264, that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 1D406, which is under tab 58, if I'm not mistaken. 1D406.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order by General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, about the assignment of zones of responsibility. Let us comment something on page 2, the second and third paragraphs from the bottom. The one I mean begins with, "The exclusive" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn the page in English, please, to find the right paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The exclusive right to command and employ units rests with the zone commander as determined by this order." And the following paragraph reads: "In the conduct of combat activities, all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander who shall decide how they are used."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, is this in line with what you stated earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is in accordance with the laws and regulations, and it also follows from the order issued by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4, line 50 -- correction 25, and page 5, line 2, Ms. Korner put it to you that the order by Colonel Lisica with regard to the police units from Prnjavor whom he ordered to come to Derventa, that this was in accordance with the setting up of the town command in Derventa. That's what she put to you. Did this order apply to the MUP members from the Prnjavor SJB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to explain in more detail. Because of the complicated and difficult situation on the front line, Commander Lisica ordered the entire police force from Derventa to be deployed to the front line urgently. He was aware that the city was left without any police, and then he ordered the Prnjavor police to send their forces to Derventa and take over police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Lisica, as you have just explained, essentially issue an order to two SJBs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He issued an order to the Derventa station about their engagement at the front line, and an order to the Prnjavor SJB to deploy police forces for policing in Derventa. Those were two orders for two stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was such an order in accordance with the rules and regulations that were in force then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both stations were in his zone of responsibility, and he acted in accordance with his powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, speaking about this, and your respective comments can be found on pages 8, 9 and 10 of today's transcript, I'll ask you about document 1D46 which is under tab 47 in the Defence binder. I apologise, it seems that I gave the wrong tab number again. I also apologise to the Trial Chamber. It's an order dated 15 May 1992. Well, then, it's all right. I apologise. You commented item 8 which is on page 2. You were asked about it by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you also gave comments on subparagraph 2 of item 8. Does this subparagraph 2 -- or, rather, let me put it this way: To which law or regulation does this subparagraph refer to? How do you understand it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This points to the measures to take against those who do not carry out the tasks they have been given, and my understanding is that this is about regular duties and tasks. And in the previous subparagraph, we can clearly see that the order says that in military operations, military regulations and rules shall be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, since Ms. Korner asked you about some hypothetical situations, allow me to ask you some questions, too. Sir, if a MUP member is at the front line in a trench, and from that place he sees that in some house or somewhere in his field of vision some persons are obviously committing a crime by breaking into that house and taking some items from it, in principle, is a police member, whenever he observes the commission of a crime during the carrying out of his regular duties, duty-bound to react if he observes the commission of a crime? I'm talking about the carrying out of the regular duties. What does the law say?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when he is carrying out his regular duties. But, if I understand you correctly, you have described a situation when the police officer was in a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get there yet. So under the law, as a MUP member, you have said that normally he is duty-bound to react. In this situation, when he is in a trench, does that MUP member -- or, rather, is that MUP member duty-bound to react or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that moment, he is carrying out a combat task, and he is duty-bound to act in the framework of the orders received when he is at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if the police officer were carrying out his regular duties in accordance with the law, and if he were to observe the commission of a crime and fails to react --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have to object. This is leading, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I understand it, he is still conducting his hypotheticals which follows the line that Ms. Korner had done in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well I'm not sure, Your Honours. He got an answer, and now he is saying "in other words," and I see that as leading, but I'll stand by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's purely hypothetical, and I'm just doing what Ms. Korner was doing half of the time this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but Ms. Korner was on cross-exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was refer together hypothetical nature of the questions, not the roles of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I was referring to the leading nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have been warned, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, when a police officer carrying out his regular duties observes or learns that the commission of a crime is in progress and fails to act, does this constitute a disciplinary offence under the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be a serious breach of his professional duties under the rule book on disciplinary responsibility that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's now refer to the second situation when he is carrying out a combat task and fails to act, although he observes the commission of a crime. Does that constitute a disciplinary offence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he is then carrying out a combat task and is duty-bound to act exclusively in line with that role of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would a MUP member who was carrying out a combat task in a trench and observes the commission of a crime and then attempt to arrest those committing a crime in accordance with his powers and duties under the Law on Internal Affairs, would he be in breach of his duties as a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At that moment and at that place, that is, at the front line, that would constitute an offence against military rules and it could even be considered desertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, we have seen your military booklet and we'll show it once more. You have the rank of captain in the armed forces, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and at some time in early 1992, I was informed that a decision -- a decision had been taken to promote me to captain 1st class but I never actually did anything to have that entered in my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is the essence of commanding the armed forces in the military the power of the commander to punish his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you are a captain in the army, you must be familiar with this. Is the following situation possible in the army: That the commander, during the performance of a combat task, has different groups of members of armed forces under him. And when I say various groups, I mean, on the one hand, those who can -- who he can command fully and punish, and so on; and, on the other hand, those on whom he cannot impose disciplinary measures or sanctions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever is part of the organic compound of a unit is under the full command of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you 1D410, tab 167. I think that this morning during cross-examination you spoke about this document to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to where that was? I can't find it in WordWheel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Page -- I'll read it out, page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked you, and I think that was the essence of her question, whether you have the order resubordinating you. And then you mentioned that there was a written order issued sometime by the end of the year, and you said that it had been commented on earlier. Tell me, is this the order that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, can we have some clarification because what I see on a screen is an order signed by Colonel Lisica. And in the page 20 and 21 where there was a reference of this, it appears to be the witness previously said he thought it was an order signed by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, it's 20, line 17: "And then the second time, it was in November 1992 when I was engaged to perform functions of the battalion commander. And in this -- and in this ... so to speak, there was no written order." I am precisely asking the witness because the record is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My apology, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke about the orders. First, there was one in spring 1992, and this is the second order, dated 11th November 1992. In this order, Commander Lisica ordered formation of a mixed battalion and then defined what is going to constitute this battalion. Under item 2, he wrote: "I hereby appoint Andrija Bjelosevic as battalion commander," that's me, "and Stijepan Pepic as deputy." And then under number 3: "Immediately carry out senior and junior command reconnaissance, assign tasks to subordinates in the field." So this is the order that was pertained to me, and I acted in accordance with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic. As I said, I would like to take a look, again, your military booklet. That's P2344 -- no, excuse me, it's P2345. It will appear on your screen in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected. 2344. P2344. I am sorry. [Interpretation] I apologise, can we have page 4, item 7. I would like to clarify something and I hope that you will be able to help us now that we have the opportunity to see this military booklet. Can we zoom in. I'm interested in item 7, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can you explain the abbreviation VES, V-E-S, as well as the number that follows immediately after? I'm talking about box number 1, training?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VES is the abbreviation for the military occupation specialty, and it had a certain number designating this particular VES. The number defines the VES, the military occupational specialty. This has to do with the officer's cadre. For instance, communications had some other number, a technical department had yet another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have to understand that some of us here are not persons to whom military terminology is entirely clear. Could you explain very briefly, what does it mean military occupational specialty? By that, I mean in simple words.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it simply, it designates what a particular conscript had been trained to do, and this specialty is then entered in his personal files, in his unit as well as in his military booklet. It means what a particular person had been trained to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if somebody is trained, for instance, to operate a mortar in artillery, that he then is assigned a particular number designated this particular military occupation specialty?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And somebody who is trained to command would then be assigned a different VES number?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers designate the coded military occupational specialty definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now page 5, number 8, promotions. Could we have the next page. I'm interested in number 6. So number 6. Thank you. Can we have the same thing in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you comment on this very briefly. I'm interested in item 6, on the basis of whose order, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would permit me, I'd like to comment on both pages very briefly. You can see that the promotion was gradual, from second lieutenant, lieutenant, and then, finally, under number 6, captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you can see that every promotion is recorded here. The rank is recorded and also on the basis of whose decree the promotion was made. The last promotion, under number 6, was done by decree of the commander of the TO of the SR BiH, and you can see the number and the date. And then I was on a war time assignment in the command of an operational JNA unit before this. You can see that the promotion, in this particular case, was made on the basis of a decree of the president of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean number 4?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can the witness be shown number 9 on the next page of the same document. Number 9 under 1. I mean number 9 that pertains to military exercises. So I'm told it's the sixth page in Serbian while we have the correct page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, could you briefly comment on numbers 1 and 2 under number 9, military exercise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This relates to the period in 1991 [as interpreted], number 1; and number 2 relates to 1983. That's when I had the war time assignment in the command of that operation unit in the command of the 327th Brigade. So this is the record of the time that I spent participating in a military exercise. Based on such exercises and evaluations, proposals for promotions would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask for a clarification. The transcript at line -- page 41, line 5, says, "this relates to the period 1991"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's for number 1 of the entry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, 1981. 1981 and 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 8 in Serbian which is number 11. I'm told it's page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a brief explanation of number 1 here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the day that I was entered into military records. It was in Derventa on the 22nd of April, 1971, so that's when I was entered into military records. After that, I was conscripted and all other things that then follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you have the rank of captain and you worked for a number of years in the National Defence Secretariat. Did all citizens, nationals, of the SFRY who were conscripted or fit for military service have same military booklets as this one?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this military training in the former SFRY an obligation for everyone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's something that stems from the concept of All People's Defence, and then, out of this concept, a system of All People's Defence was developed. So there was the army, that is the operative part of the structure, and then there was Territorial Defence. There were different units classified to different principles. Then there were units of social self-protection that comprised also the civilian protection units. It was something that was defined in the constitution. The constitution said that the defence of the country was both right and obligation of all citizens. And in accordance to that, there was also a duty to train the civilian population, for instance, for evacuation, protection, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did every individual have the right and duty to respond and attend military exercises just like you did twice?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone had a duty to respond to such a call and to report to the place of his war time assignment. It could have been a mobilisational exercise or simple training, but everyone had the duty to respond to such call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, I found the document that we mentioned awhile ago. So for completeness sake, I would like you to comment on it. It's tab 61, 65 ter 544D1. Excuse me, I'm told it's tab 120. I have no idea why I have tab 61 written here. Could I have your brief comment on this. What is it and what is it about? I apologise, forgive me, Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm being told now that you should look at the monitor. I was right, after all, it was tab 61, not 120.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the order of the commander of Tactical Group 3, Commander Lisica, whereby he orders that certain forces be set up and he uses the jargon word for police, he says "gendarmerie." That is what he means. To use the "gendarmerie" forces from Derventa, Prnjavor and then a company of the Naradzic, Rajko Battalion, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this Lieutenant Jankovic who is supposed to be the commander of that unit, was he a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was part of the town command, and by way of his order, he directly re-subordinated these police forces. He -- by putting them at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when military administration is introduced -- I can show you the relevant document later on, but you let me ask you this first: If military administration is being introduced, is it the commander who designates the officer to be in charge of the public security station and police in a particular town?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If military administration is being introduced, and if a commander is being designated as the town commander, then all structures who are located there, be it that they just find themselves there or that they are being established by way of the order of that commander, all of these structures, all of these forces are being put under the command of the town commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If there are no objections, I would like to have this document tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure specifically how this arises or relates to the cross-examine. I'm working at a disadvantage here because you know I came in cold off the bench this morning, so I may have missed where it comes from. But if it's going to be admitted, I would request my learned friend make some clarification because in the witness's answer at page 43, line 11 he said, "Yes," referring to Lieutenant Jankovic, "he was part of the town command, and by way of his order he directly subordinated these police forces." This isn't Jankovic's order. So either that answer is incorrect, or he is referring to some other document than the one that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please clarify. I don't want to repeat the question, and it is not entirely clear what Mr. Hannis is objecting.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what the transcript says, then my words were not recorded properly. I said by way of this order, town commander Jankovic had this unit put directly under his command, the unit comprising the company under the command of Naradzic. So these forces were established by way of the order of the commander of the tactical group, and these forces were directly put under the command of Lieutenant Jankovic by way of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this is a satisfactory explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For reference of the Trial Chamber, the documents mentioned by Ms. Korner concerning introduction of military administration in Derventa municipality and concerning the appointment of acting chief of the SJB, are 1D480, 1D408.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, on page 12 of today's transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are not sure whether the first document mentioned was 1D480 or 1D470.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When answering the question of Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know if my learned friend heard, but the interpreters said they had a question about whether the first document mentioned at page 45, line 3, was 1D480 or 1D470. I wonder if we could have a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I'm sorry. I'm rushing because of the time. There are two documents I wanted to put on the record for the benefit of all. It's 1D470 and 1D408. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, on page 12 -- actually, it started on page 11 and continued on to page 12, you spoke about some situations when the military commander handed down some punishments to policemen and then we went into private session to mention the names of some of these people.
