Then on page 12, you said how you could remember two such cases and then you described them, and then Ms. Korner asked you -- or, rather, she interrupted you and she said, No, no, I want something else. You said that they were arrested and that is not the same. I wish to know what disciplinary or criminal proceedings were instituted against these people. Then you said that the military had a different system and that this was what you were trying to explain. I gave you the context of this issue that was discussed previously. Now, let me ask you this: Does the army fall under the Law on State Administration?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the army does not fall under that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does the army have a disciplinary proceedings that could be considered identical as the one that exists with relation to members of the MUP and as regulated by the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Public servants, policemen, and so on, they all fall under the Law on State Administration plus the specific laws, such as the Law on Internal Affairs which regulates the work of policemen, and so on. As for the army, their legal framework consists of the Law on National Defence, Law on Service in Armed Forces, and this is a separate system. The commander is the person who metes out punishment or measures to members of the army and all of those who are in the process of carrying out a military assignment. When it comes to state administration and police, there are all sorts of disciplinary commissions. There are disciplinary proceedings that have completely different elements and rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Therefore, I think you have replied, but let us be fully clear. Other disciplinary commissions, disciplinary proceedings and disciplinary organs in the army, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It functioned in accordance with unity of command and singleness of command principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on military rules, who is authorised to send somebody into military detention?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be done at the level of the company commander and higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this punishment of military detention, was it meted out in relation to members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, Mr. Bjelosevic, just one or two more questions about what was discussed today, and then we will move on to topics that were covered previously. Today on page 17, line 7, Ms. Korner asked you about the order that you received from Mr. Stanisic in 1994 when he served as minister for the second time. You started explaining this to us and then on page 17, line 7, you said, no, this is something that happened in 1994. This is when he gave me this task. I was supposed to go to Prijedor. I think it was sometime in April. We had to solve the multiple murder where 16 or 17 people were killed. And this is where Ms. Korner interrupted you. Tell us what this was about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I started explaining --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I object it's not relevant. She didn't interrupt. He answered when she asked at line 11 on page 17: "Sorry, this is a killing that took place in 1994?" Answer: "Yes." Then she said: "Don't worry about that. It's outside what we are concerned about." So I don't see how this arises from cross-examination or how it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can take off his earphones and then I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Korner was citing this paragraph, was asking this question because of the contents of the interview of Mr. Mico Stanisic which is a P exhibit. I will give you the reference. I mentioned it in my opening statement. It's actually a couple of exhibit numbers. Now, this, this question goes into the credibility of what Mr. Stanisic was saying, and therefore because it was misinterpreted by Ms. Korner, I have to ask this question of this witness because it was she who opened this question by posing it. And now I have to clarify it, Your Honour, because, by this, it could be understood that the witness agrees with her suggestion which is completely misinterpretation of what was said in the interview. Now, I want to clarify this situation very shortly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But we're still dealing with matters in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I need some clarification because Mr. Zecevic seemed to be saying that Ms. Korner misinterpreted something from Mr. Stanisic's testimony that's in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his interview that's in evidence, P2303.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where he --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where he talks about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where it recorded that he ordered this witness to conduct an investigation into the Koricanske cliff killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that not what it says in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in the transcript, but it doesn't say so in the interview. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this is not the witness to do it with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness denied that. He said he never got that order. So what is the problem? And Ms. Korner didn't insist. And she didn't want to know about the killing in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand and appreciate. I'm sorry, Your Honours. It was my misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can put the headphones back on. No need to answer this question because we have resolved this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask that we take the break now, Your Honours, because I'm ready to move to the previous phase. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered in, I was doing some preliminary inquiries about the possibility that we sit longer today for half an hour, if possible, if I can -- because I would like to finish with the witness today, if possible. But I informed Ms. Veretelnikova that I would be able to give the firm assessment only at 1.30 because at that point I will know whether I can finish within additional half an hour. If not, then we will have to continue tomorrow with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So between now and then, the usual inquiries would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, on page 20785 through -790, on the first day of your cross-examination, you commented on your diaries and official notebooks for Ms. Korner. You may remember answering the Prosecutor's question whether you had notes from meetings that you had with General Talic or anybody else. You replied in the negative. This may be a good opportunity to remind ourselves that during military exercises before the war, we received military notebooks, and you will see in my military booklet that I took part this those exercises. When the exercise finished, we were duty-bound to return the official notebooks before returning home. Those were the rules that were in force in the army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, does the Law on Internal Affairs contain any duties of MUP members to have such official notebooks?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does every military officer have an official notebook in army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And once the official notebook is full, what must the officer do with that notebook?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must return it. Either when the notebook is full or when the mission is accomplished, and before he leaves, but certainly there was an obligation to return it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To return it to who?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command where it was issued. Before leaving, all military documents had to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And those military documents, as far as you know, if you know, where were they kept after that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when I was in the brigade command that it was kept in a separate locker in the command, and when we would come there again for military exercise, then we would again be issued the notebooks. And upon completion of the exercise, we would return them. Where those documents eventually ended up, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the same in 1992 when you were first re-subordinated to the JNA and then to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Upon completion of the task I was assigned, I had to return all my -- all the military documents and the equipment that I received when I got my military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 20816 through -819, a document was shown to you. It's under tab 2 of the Prosecution binder. It's 65 ter 20000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that this is the transcript of an intercept. The conversation that was intercepted was one between Radovan Karadzic and Branko Ostojic. We've already spoken about this. Ms. Korner put it to you that -- what we can see on the first page towards the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down. In Serbian it's the correct page but it's on the following page of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, Ms. Korner put it to you that the words, "He is a good man," uttered by Branko Ostojic and Karadzic's reply, "Excellent, we need a professional." As well as the comment by Ostojic, "He is a real one." And Karadzic's words that follow, "We need a professional," that all these refer to you. When you read this transcript, do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm being advised that what Ms. Korner put to him has not been correctly stated. Can we have a precise reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I gave the reference to the pages 20816 to 20819, and Ms. Korner says: "Now, this is July, a couple of months after you've been appointed at CSB Doboj. Do you have any idea on what basis Mr. Karadzic is calling you 'Andrija' and saying what an excellent fellow you are?" Then I made the -- then I made the objection, and then Ms. Korner said: "Well, I'm sorry, this is a matter of comment and an improper one, I may say, Mr. Zecevic." And then she quotes the exact parts which I quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't see the basis of the -- Mr. Hannis's interjection that it inaccurately reflects what was put it him, but what I do have difficulty with is Mr. Zecevic's question, "When you read this question transcript, do you agree with that proposition?" It seems, among other thing, it's really unfair to the witness. You are inviting his comment on his own abilities by two persons who had a conversation just referring to him. I don't know how helpful any answer he gives would be. As I said, it strikes me as being unfair to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the witness is unable to answer, he may say so. I'm not trying to be unfair to him, I'm just trying to clarify the situation. Because in my understanding of the Serbian language, it is very clear to whom this refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, when you said, "Do you agree with the proposition," perhaps I'm misunderstanding the question, but what I interpret it to mean is whether he agrees with the proposition attributed in the intercept of Karadzic, "Excellent we immediate a professional," et cetera, where Ostojic said, "He is a good man." That's what I said seems to be unfair to put the witness in a position of agreeing with that, but perhaps your question is not as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess that would be my request, Your Honour. If the question could be reformulated because the way I heard a question, when the answer is no, one interpretation of that is the witness is saying, No I don't agree that they said I was a good man, because I wasn't a good man, perhaps. I don't think that's what he meant but the way the question is formulated, it's difficult to understand what the answer means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that. I will reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, I have read out this part of the intercepted conversation. Can you tell us who these comments refer to, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this carefully and my conclusion is the following: That Mr. Ostojic is asking Mr. Karadzic about some person, and this could be interpreted as an intervention to hire someone, but the name is not mentioned. And then the way I understand it, Karadzic tells Ostojic that this person should contact me in Doboj, and he is praising that person as a good man, a professional. And Mr. Karadzic is saying, "Excellent, we need a professional." That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do these comments refer to that person or to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand them to refer to that person they talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. On page 20865 through -68 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, before we go on, could I request that the Court perhaps ask my learned friend to inquire of the witness whether he has only read the transcript or actually listened to the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much turns on this, Mr. Hannis. Ms. Korner had an understanding of it. She questioned the witness on it. Mr. Zecevic has a different take and we have an answer. I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber would make such sense of it as it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D135. I think that's under tab 18 in the Defence binder. 1D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the pages I cited, you commented on this -- on this summary of the minutes of a meeting held in Banja Luka on 11 February 1992. You remember that you commented on this for Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And she -- or, rather, you read on page 2 in Serbian, something that is on page 1 in English, I mean, the -- Mico Stanisic's words that a list of minimal outstanding demands should be assembled at this meeting and submitted to Minister Alija Delimustafic. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner put to you that this conclusion is not mentioned among the other conclusions, namely that these demands should be submitted to Minister Delimustafic with a dead-line for the resolution among other things because this was a secret meeting in Banja Luka which you attended. Please take a look at page 4 of this document. And focus on Mr. Malko Koroman's comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were present at this meeting. Do you remember the words of Mr. Koroman?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Koroman took a radical stand. It may even be called an ultimatum, and he wanted to cut the whole meeting short. It boils down to, Okay, we have established what we need and we must submit a demand to get that, and if that demand is not met, then we'll block roads, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page 5 in Serbian. We can stay on the same page in English, and -- I mean, the comment of Mr. Nedjo Vlaski. Do you remember what he said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember Nedjo and his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Vlaski advocated strong media support and informing the public of the demands formulated at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a number of people participating in the discussion who emphasised the need to go into the media with this. They considered that it was possible to exert greater pressure on Minister Delimustafic and his associates through the media and then the demands would be met.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 20865 and -868, Ms. Korner suggested reasons because of which Zepinic did not attend the meeting. She asked you on page 20869 and -870 whether you informed Mr. Zepinic about your complaints. The day before we saw in your diary that you met Mr. Zepinic on the 10th of February as well as Delimustafic. And your reply was: "I told him on a number of occasions before he went to Sarajevo and also through the phone. Every time when he promised that he would solve the problem, he would complain that the chief of the personnel department had been replaced, and Vesinovic [phoen] left, Srebrenikovic arrived, and he was the one who pulled all the strings and that nothing could be done at the moment." This answer is not quite clear in the transcript. Could you please explain what you were referring to when you said those words. And who are those people, Vesinovic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesinovic must be a misprint. It's Hilmo Selimovic. He was the assistant minister for personnel, if I remember correctly, until the autumn 1991 or the fall of 1991. He was replaced by Srebrenikovic. So these are the names. Now, what did I say about this? I put forward a number of proposals for different appointments as well as proposals to obtain certain technical equipment for the service. You can see that in my notebooks. Very often at meetings with my own associates, I discussed those subjects. I also made for myself an aide-memoire before I went to the ministry in Sarajevo so that I would know what I had to request there. But it took ages and finally it wasn't resolved, and that's what I was talking about. Now, the lack of efficiency and this personal blockade, so to speak, made me conclude, in the end, that Mr. Zepinic had neither the power nor personality to resolve that, and he confirmed it to me at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. Did Mr. Zepinic complain to you that because of the replacement of Mr. Selimovic, he was not in a position to ensure that the things that had been requested for him be realised in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he told me twice to go and contact another department chief. I think the name was Hajra Hodzic. He told me to speak to him directly and try to obtain what I needed from him. Hajra received me very politely and courteously and we spoke, but he clearly told me without the approval of Assistant Chief Srebrenikovic, he could not do a thing because those were his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20900 and -901, you were shown document P439. That's Prosecution tab 11 bis. And it's stenographic minutes of the Assembly of RS held on Pale on the 24th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show to the witness page 31 in Serbian. ERN number is 0089-6886.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that you commented on this? Ms. Korner read some excerpts from this stenograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to comment on the first paragraph and the second paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to the English page, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'm trying to find in the transcript. Thirteen, I guess, in the e-court. That's what Ms. Korner says. We have the correct Serbian page. No, no, we had the correct Serbian page. The English page was -- the Serbian page is 31 and the English should be 13. Sorry, we have the wrong English page. I'm reading from the transcript what Ms. Korner was saying and that is why I am ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that this was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just wait until we find it in English. [In English] It's the speech of Dr. Karadzic. [Interpretation] It could be page 17 in English. Yes, it's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The two paragraphs that I want you to comment on which are positioned at the top of the page in Serbian. In English, they are two paragraphs from the bottom beginning with words, "Newly-established municipalities." Now we have it on the screen, so could you comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is already the time when many paramilitary units had been established in the field, and also they were known to the public. That is also the time when barricades had been erected, so seen within this context, I think that this is a request to establish the forces in those newly-formed municipalities who were supposed to prevent any threats directed at the territory, any incursions of armed forces, and they speak here about mini-vans. If I can remember that time correctly, this probably relates to the transport of large quantities of dinar bank notes which were then transported from Croatia, literally, in mini-vans. That money was used to buy foreign currency in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was then taken out of the country. And if you read my notes, as well as informative bulletins, that there was a lot of attention given to this particular issue in our area because we wanted to prevent the foreign currency leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was then the position of Mr. Karadzic on two issues here, that is the freedom of movement of citizens and the public order?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he underlines that these measures would not endanger the freedom of movement. And also he says peace at any cost, wherever it is possible. I see that he is very worried about the events in Gorazde. He says that it's very dangerous, that it is necessary to avoid it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the context of this speech by Karadzic and it's interpretation by Ms. Korner on page 20903 up to 20905, she linked up the events in Doboj on the 2nd and 3rd of May and the speech by Mr. Karadzic at this Assembly session on the 24th of March. You responded to that. However, part of your reply at 20903 contains the following words: "If you permit me, I would like to clarify the situation. The events in Doboj occurred between the 2nd and 3rd of May. However, before that in March, there was the take-over of the public security station which was carried out by HOS and other paramilitary groups in Bosanski Brod." Can you explain what you were referring to here? What is HOS and what other paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I already spoke about the paramilitary formation that existed in that period of time. Now, if we talk specifically about Brod, there were forces organised there which went to the battle-field in Croatia already in 1991, and their strength was growing. Later on, there were also Croatian Armed Forces. I think I also mentioned that Anto Prkacin appeared in a TV show, and I brought this video on a CD, so you can see that he explains in detail how he executed the action of the take-over of the public security station in Brod which he did, as he put it, with his men. And that's when he --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was: "What is HOS and what are the other paramilitary groups?" This answer is going far beyond the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just make it short, Mr. Bjelosevic, I agree.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were paramilitary formations, as I have already said. There was the Patriotic League, there were units within the HDZ which were practically the extended arm of the National Guards Corps units and they were also the Green Berets, plus the units that had crossed over from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, further in that same answer, you say: "Then the station in Derventa was taken over. We also had the situation in Odzak. And then in some parts, there were camps set up where civilians were being held. The same happened in Modrica. So we basically had the situation, which, for all intents and purposes, meant the occupation of the territory. The camps had already been established, population already expelled from some parts, civilian population. And it was only after that that the decision was made that Doboj should at least be spared of that same fate, that we should prevent these same events taking place in Doboj." You mentioned camps in two places. You also mentioned civilians being expelled. I would like to ask you this: Which camps did you have in mind? Who had set them up and who held them? And members of which ethnic community did you refer to when you spoke of civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a compound question with about five parts. Could we take them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer one at a time. Which camps? Who set them up? And the third question was members of which ethnic community did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitary forces in the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the units that had come from Croatia took over the public security station and the bridge, crossed over and started taking up territory. They took the city of Bosanski Brod and then started attacking villages, one by one, which resulted in population being expelled, refugees, and so on. This wave spread from Doboj -- from Brod to Derventa and down south. And then a camp was set up at the Polet [phoen] stadium, and the forces that I have enumerated held the captured Serb population there. The next camp was set up in Tulek, in the town itself. And then, later on, in April, a camp was set up in Derventa by those same forces, and Serb civilians were held there. Later on, there was a camp in Radic [phoen] where there were military facilities and hangars. And subsequently, another camp was set up in Polje where there were silos where the feed mill was. Whereas in Odzak, there was a camp in a plant called Stolit [phoen]. And then, later on, there were even other instances of mass capture of Serb civilians and then the camp was set up in an elementary school. So this wave was moving closer to Doboj. And the JNA issued an explicit order that Doboj should be protected and control of it maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, let me ask you this first: The situation that you just described in your answer, did that cause fear in Doboj, these facts that you just enumerated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. A huge number of refugees came from the northern part to Banja Luka and to Doboj. People brought with themselves these stories about what they had experienced. Those who didn't manage to flee were sent to camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier that the JNA issued an explicit order that Doboj should be protected and that they should keep Doboj under their control. So tell me, please, who was the commander of the JNA garrison in Doboj at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant-Colonel Cazim Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, but I think that he declared himself as a Yugoslav, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point, Ms. Korner asked you about Mr. Stankovic, and you said that Stankovic was a major at the time. What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Stankovic arrived in 1991, arrived in Doboj. To tell you the truth, I don't know his exact establishment position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on page 20908 and -909, you discussed with Ms. Korner the dispatch of the 31st of March, 1991, signed by Assistant Minister Momcilo Mandic. P353. In your reply, you said the following: "It is quite clear what is being said here. However, I have to tell you that after this dispatch there was a series of dispatches, that it had been agreed and that a collegium was held with Minister Delimustafic, and then there were denials that it took place, so the situation was quite confusing. Therefore, at that point in time it wasn't practically possible to understand what situation would be ultimately. Something was going on, everything was possible, and so on." I wish to show you a document that we received from the OTP, in the meantime. That is to say, I didn't show it to you before. And following that, this document was shown to another witness for the first time. This is 2320 MFI'd. So I would like you to tell us whether you know this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers. I have an objection. It's my understanding this was not on the original list of documents the Defence intended to use with the witness. It seems clearly it's something that they could have done so. I received notice, I don't know, 15, 20 minutes ago that they were now proposing to add it to their list. I'm not sure to what aspect of cross-examination it goes to and why it wasn't on their list before. It has been marked as P2320 MFI. If Mr. Zecevic want to have it received in evidence without the MFI, then I'm willing to do it and have him talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I am opposed to him using it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, of course I can't anticipate what will the cross-examination of the witness bring, what issues will be discussed between the cross-examining party and the witness. Once they finish their cross-examination, then I can add some documents and for the redirect, and clearly this has been a situation in a number of occasions in the past when the Office of the Prosecutor were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm inclined to agree, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, but you haven't addressed the issue of why it wasn't on their list before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as Mr. Zecevic -- well, first of all, we haven't heard the precise question as being put, but as Mr. Zecevic just said, is that the nature of the whole forensic exercise is such that the utility or relevance of a particular document may only become apparent after, in this case, the cross-examination. So I don't know that -- how we can impose a rule on him to -- that would not permit him to use this document, the relevance of which is only now apparently become apparent. I hate to sound redundant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I do understand that, Your Honour and I've certainly been on the other side of that situation myself. However, he has directed this witness to his testimony on the 19th of May at page 20908. That's been several days ago, and it seems like if he was aware of it, he could have given us notice before this morning that it was something he intended to use or wanted to add to his list. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could we have a tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a tab number, Your Honour. I just added it. I am sorry. It's the document that we have on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But it is on the Prosecutor's list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was on our list to use with Defence expert, Mr. Bajagic, was the first time it appeared on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember this document? Can you tell us anything about it, whether you ever received it, whether you are familiar at all with this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the great number of dispatches, and, as I have told you, there were all kinds of writings indicating that, yes, a collegium had been held and then it was denied, and then again we received information that it had been held. So I'm not sure. I recognise some of these signatures, but right now I couldn't remember. I don't want to improvise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking you to acknowledge this document. I am just asking you whether you ever received it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 20910 and -911, you discussed with Ms. Korner your diary. And she asked you about the meeting held on the 11th of July in Belgrade, the first meeting, collegium. No, first it was the meeting in February and the dispatch from Mr. Mandic. I apologise. I gave you the wrong reference. It is 20909. So between the meeting held on the 11th of February and this dispatch of Mr. Mandic, Ms. Korner wanted to know whether you had attended a meeting in Sarajevo with other high officials of the Serbian MUP. You answered no. Then she asked you, or rather, she referred you to the words of Mr. Zupljanin uttered at the meeting in July where Mr. Zupljanin, according to Ms. Korner, said something to the effect that, It's been a long time since we met in Sarajevo. Then she asked you again whether you had a meeting in Sarajevo, and you replied that you didn't remember meeting in Sarajevo under those circumstances, in that composition, and so on. Sir, in your diary, do you have an entry about the meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness answered, but the interpreter is asking him to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. It wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know until I take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will clearly not be able to finish today. So, therefore, I don't think it makes sense that we ask for additional half an hour sitting today. We will have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I entered this in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I saw it somewhere, but I'll get back to it tomorrow when we return to the issue of your diary. Mr. Bjelosevic --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, I apologise. 11292 BL which stands for Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but we'll deal with it tomorrow. Just one more question: Did you enter all meetings you considered important in your diary?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, a hypothetical question: If such a meeting had taken place in Sarajevo, would you have entered it in your diary?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 20911 through -13, you commented on document 1D455 for Ms. Korner. That's at tab 31 in the OTP binder. You are about to see the document on your screen. It's an invitation sent out to the SJBs to come to a meeting in Doboj on 1 April 1992. You commented on it with Ms. Korner. I'm asking you this just in order to clarify the transcript, which, to my mind, was somewhat unclear with regard to your answer. Ms. Korner put to you that this meeting had something to do with Mr. Mandic's dispatch, dated 31 March, but you denied that. So now tell us: Who sent out this letter on your behalf and what was his position in the Doboj CSB?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch was signed by Mr. Vojo Blagojevic, who was chief of the department of the police. The commanders of police stations were under his direct authority due to the line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's good that you told us that. Tell us so that we understand better, what is the hierarchy in public security stations or police stations? Who is number one, who is number two and so on? But we only need the three highest ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station is run by the station chief. The second -- second highest ranking in the hierarchy is the commander of the police station. And if there was a traffic police station, then there was also the commander of that station. That was under his direct authority and according to the line of work. Well, there was also the crime enforcement detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So there's a connection according to the line of work. This connection between the executive personnel of the SJBs and the -- on one hand, and the CSB on the other, how -- what was it like exactly? To who did the SJB commanders report according to the line of work?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders reported to the department of the police, if we are speaking about the line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the chief of the department of the police at the CSB has authority over the commanders of SJBs in the territory according to the line of work?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were subordinate to him and reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more clarification about this document. Paragraph 2 reads: "SM and SMBS commanders must attend the meeting." You have just explained who the SM commanders are, do explain the abbreviation SMBS.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SMBS stands for traffic police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic. Sir, when there's a meeting of people in the same line of work, does that mean, in principle, that the chief of the CSB attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends. It was not mandatory, but he could attend the meeting depending on the topics to be dealt with and the agenda, his -- whether he had time available, other commitments, et cetera. Certainly he was not duty-bound to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Ms. Korner insisted that you say whether you and your executive officials at the CSB had a meeting after the dispatch dated 31 March which was sent out by Momcilo Mandic, to which question you answered in the negative saying, "No, I never held such a meeting." And then on page 20918, you explained by saying: "I do not agree with you. During that period, I made every effort to preserve a stable situation and peace, and you can call it whatever you please. Up until that moment, I had the opportunity to see what was happening in the territories affected by the war. I saw what was happening to the victims and refugees and all the evils of war. That is why I wanted to preserve the peace." Mr. Bjelosevic, when you said that you saw what was happening in the war zone and what was happening with the victims and refugees and all the evils of war, what exactly did you have in mind, but very briefly, please? Which time-period and which territory were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, I had in mind what was happening in the area around Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Odzak, and so on, and the horrible things people were going through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I may be able to use the remaining time for a couple of questions. On page 20935 through -40, Ms. Korner showed you the Law on Internal Affairs which is P530 here, and it's at tab 10A of the Defence binder. You are about to see the document on your screen. What we are interested in is page 2 of the Serbian version, Article 10 of the law. Then Ms. Korner asked you about Article 10. And on page 20935, you answered: "Yes, in the police jargon this was called 'assistance.' Like, for example, some other government bodies must carry out a decision of, say, the inspectorate when we talk about a construction project, for example. And the construction inspectorate prohibits the construction of a building and orders that what has already been built must be demolished. Then the police, in such a case, provides assistance to able the construction inspectorate to demolish that building or part of the building." Sir, is the police duty-bound to provide such assistance only to bodies that exercise public authority or any state body?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who enforce the law and in the process meet with resistance on the part of those to who the law is applied. So if somebody is unable to enforce their decision, then you apply for assistance to the police and the police can help them do their job. We are talking about various institutions, not only inspectorates. For example, the social welfare centre or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're introduction was good. But is the police duty bound under the law to provide assistance to enforce a court decision, for example?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The example you gave where a court decides that a child be given to one parent for custody, but the child is currently in the custody of the other parent, does the executive body of the court apply for assistance from the police if they have reason to assume that there will be problems of any kind? And is the police duty-bound to act in accordance with such an application?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When a court issues such an application, the police is duty-bound to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last paragraph of Article 10 which says that before reaching a decision as outlined in the preceding paragraph, the consent of the minister must be obtained. As far as you know, was the chief of an SJB always duty-bound to apply for consent of the minister or only in such cases when, according to his assessment, there could be physical resistance or use of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon reception of a request for assistance, an assessment is made, a risk assessment with regard to the enforcement of that decision. And it is exactly as it is stated here. If the assessment is that there could be more massive resistance or even armed resistance, then the station chief is duty-bound to inform the superior official and apply for approval or consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this provision of the law apply only to assistants as request by other state bodies that exercise public powers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in all other cases, does the police act pursuant to the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic, we will have to continue tomorrow. I know that you have been here for quite awhile but I promise we will certainly finish tomorrow before the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning. And we are in this courtroom for the entirety of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.
